subject: Compiler Construction (Full Syllabus)
description: Front-end of the compiler: introduction and language-processing tools, lexical analysis (regular expressions and finite automata), syntax analysis (context-free grammars and top-down/bottom-up parsing), and semantic analysis with syntax-directed translation.

questions.text: The main reason for using an intermediate representation in a compiler is to:
options: Make it possible to reuse the front-end with different target machines
questions.shortExplanation: IR decouples the front-end from the back-end.
questions.explanation: An intermediate representation lets the same front-end be reused with different back-ends, separating machine-independent analysis from machine-dependent code generation.

questions.text: A preprocessor is typically responsible for:
options: Allocating registers to variables in the program
Generating final machine code for the target
questions.shortExplanation: Preprocessors handle macros and file inclusion.
questions.explanation: A preprocessor performs textual transformations such as macro expansion and including other source files before actual compilation begins.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a phase of a compiler?
questions.shortExplanation: Editing is not a compiler phase.
questions.explanation: Lexical analysis, semantic analysis, and intermediate code generation are compiler phases; text editing is an external activity, not part of compilation.

questions.text: The number of passes of a compiler refers to:
options: The number of tokens it produces
The count of registers it uses
The number of errors it tolerates
How many times it traverses the source or its representation
questions.shortExplanation: A pass is one complete traversal of the program.
questions.explanation: A pass is a single traversal over the source program or an intermediate form; a multi-pass compiler traverses the representation more than once.

questions.text: Unlike a compiler, an interpreter:
options: Produces a standalone executable that runs without the interpreter present
questions.shortExplanation: Interpreters execute directly without separate target code.
questions.explanation: An interpreter processes and executes the source program statement by statement, without producing a separate target program.

questions.text: Just-in-time (JIT) compilation generally takes place:
options: Only on a different machine than the target
Before the program source has even been written by the developer
questions.explanation: A JIT compiler translates code (often bytecode) into machine code while the program is running, combining interpretation flexibility with compiled speed.

questions.text: Resolving references between separately compiled modules is the job of the:
options: Lexical analyzer that scans the source
questions.explanation: The linker combines object modules and resolves external symbols (such as functions defined in one file and used in another) into a single program.

questions.text: A compiler that emits assembly language as its output still requires a(n):
options: Interpreter to execute it statement by statement
questions.shortExplanation: An assembler converts assembly to machine code.
questions.explanation: If a compiler emits assembly language, an assembler is required to translate that assembly into relocatable machine code.

questions.text: Placing an executable into memory and starting its execution is performed by the:
options: Code optimizer that improves the program
questions.shortExplanation: The loader places the program in memory.
questions.explanation: A loader copies the executable into memory, adjusts addresses if needed, and prepares it for execution.

questions.text: Three-address code is best classified as a(n):
options: Token type produced by the scanner
Parsing technique used by the parser
questions.explanation: Three-address code is a common intermediate representation in which each instruction has at most three operands, used between analysis and code generation.

questions.text: Which part of a compiler is generally machine-independent?
options: Register allocation for the target processor
questions.explanation: Lexical, syntax, and semantic analysis depend on the source language, not the target machine, making the front-end machine-independent.

questions.text: A compiler written in the very language it compiles is said to be:
options: A cross-compiler that runs on a separate host machine
questions.shortExplanation: Self-hosting compilers compile their own language.
questions.explanation: A self-hosting compiler is implemented in the very language it translates, a situation enabled through bootstrapping.

questions.text: A source-to-source translator (transpiler) produces:
options: Relocatable machine code for the processor
questions.explanation: A source-to-source compiler translates one high-level language into another high-level language rather than into machine code.

questions.text: In a typical language-processing system, which tool runs immediately before the assembler?
options: The loader that brings the program into memory
questions.explanation: The typical pipeline is preprocessor → compiler (emitting assembly) → assembler → linker/loader, so the compiler precedes the assembler.

questions.text: Which statement about the symbol table is correct?
options: It is built only after code generation finishes
It is used only by the scanner
It is shared and updated by several compiler phases
It stores the final target machine code of the program
questions.shortExplanation: Multiple phases share the symbol table.
questions.explanation: The symbol table records identifier information and is created and used across lexical, syntactic, semantic, and later phases.

questions.text: Dynamic linking means library code is linked:
options: During lexical analysis of the program
Before the source program is compiled at all
At load time or run time
Only by the assembler in pass one
questions.shortExplanation: Dynamic linking happens at load/run time.
questions.explanation: With dynamic linking, shared library references are resolved when the program is loaded or while it runs, instead of being copied in at build time.

questions.text: Reporting diagnostics and recovering so analysis can continue is the role of the:
options: Register allocator that assigns machine registers
questions.shortExplanation: The error handler manages diagnostics and recovery.
questions.explanation: The error-handling component reports diagnostics and applies recovery strategies so the compiler can keep processing the rest of the program.

questions.text: Using an invalid character such as '@' where it is not allowed is detected during:
questions.explanation: When the scanner cannot match the input against any valid token pattern, it reports a lexical error.

questions.text: Java source code is usually compiled first into:
options: Native machine code only, with no virtual machine involved
questions.explanation: Java source is compiled to portable bytecode that is then executed (interpreted or JIT-compiled) by the Java Virtual Machine.

questions.text: Which of the following is produced last in the compilation process?
options: A stream of tokens from the scanner
questions.shortExplanation: Machine code is the final product.
questions.explanation: Tokens, parse trees, and the symbol table are intermediate; the target machine code is generated at the end of the back-end.

questions.text: A grouping of compiler phases into one traversal of the program is called a:
options: Token recognized by the lexical analyzer
questions.explanation: Several phases may be combined into a single pass, where a pass reads the input once and writes an output once.

questions.text: Which activity belongs to the synthesis (back-end) stage?
options: Building the parse tree from the token stream
questions.explanation: Synthesis takes the intermediate representation and produces the target program; tokenizing and parsing belong to analysis.

questions.text: Compared with compiled code, interpreted execution is usually:
options: Always completely free of runtime errors
Faster but much harder to debug at the source level
questions.explanation: Interpretation tends to run slower because translation happens at run time, but it offers easier, more immediate error reporting and debugging.

questions.text: A compiler driver (toolchain front program) is responsible for:
options: Invoking the preprocessor, compiler, assembler, and linker in sequence
questions.explanation: The compiler driver coordinates the separate tools of the language-processing system so the user can invoke them with a single command.

questions.text: Translating assembly language into relocatable machine code is the task of the:
options: Loader that copies the program into main memory
questions.shortExplanation: The assembler handles assembly to machine code.
questions.explanation: An assembler converts low-level assembly mnemonics into relocatable machine instructions and produces an object file.

questions.text: Which is the correct ordering of the first three analysis phases?
options: Semantic analysis, then lexical analysis, then syntax analysis
Syntax analysis, then lexical analysis, then semantic analysis
questions.explanation: Scanning produces tokens, parsing builds structure, and then semantic analysis checks meaning, so the order is lexical, syntax, semantic.

questions.text: A type mismatch between an integer and a string is detected during:
options: Lexical analysis of the character stream
questions.explanation: Type checking is part of semantic analysis, which verifies that operations are applied to operands of compatible types.

questions.text: A two-pass assembler uses its first pass primarily to:
options: Optimize the assembly program for speed
Generate the final machine code for every instruction
Build the symbol table of labels
questions.explanation: The first pass of a two-pass assembler scans the source to assign addresses and record labels in a symbol table; the second pass emits code.

questions.text: A missing semicolon at the end of a statement is most likely reported during:
questions.explanation: A missing semicolon violates the grammar of the language, so it is detected by the parser during syntax analysis.

questions.text: The main benefit of splitting a compiler into a front-end and a back-end is:
options: It removes the need for a symbol table entirely
It allows reuse across languages and machines
It eliminates all possible runtime errors in programs
questions.shortExplanation: Front/back split enables retargeting and reuse.
questions.explanation: With a shared intermediate representation, one front-end can target many machines and one back-end can serve many languages.

questions.text: The smallest meaningful unit returned by the scanner is a:
questions.explanation: The lexical analyzer groups characters into tokens, the smallest meaningful syntactic units passed to the parser.

questions.text: A pattern, in lexical analysis, is:
options: A rule describing the lexemes a token can represent
A node of the parse tree
questions.shortExplanation: A pattern is the rule for a token's lexemes.
questions.explanation: A pattern (often a regular expression) describes the form that the lexemes of a particular token may take; an actual matched string is a lexeme.

questions.text: The token attribute value for an identifier is usually:
options: Its line of generated object code
A pointer to its symbol-table entry
Its absolute machine address in memory
questions.shortExplanation: Identifier tokens carry a symbol-table pointer.
questions.explanation: For identifiers, the scanner records an attribute that points to the symbol-table entry holding the identifier's information.

questions.text: Two-buffer input with sentinels is used by the scanner to:
options: Resolve ambiguity in the grammar of the language
Optimize the use of machine registers
Reduce the size of the parse tree
Speed up reading of source characters
questions.explanation: Two-buffer schemes with a sentinel character reduce the number of tests and I/O operations the scanner performs while reading the source.

questions.text: A sentinel in input buffering is:
options: A special marker placed at the end of a buffer half
A reserved keyword of the source language
An accepting state of the automaton
questions.explanation: A sentinel is a special character (such as EOF) placed at the end of each buffer half so a single test can detect both end-of-buffer and end-of-input.

questions.text: The positive closure operator (+) applied to r denotes:
options: One or more occurrences of r
An optional single occurrence of r
Zero or more occurrences of the expression r
questions.explanation: Positive closure r+ matches one or more concatenations of r, equivalent to r r*.

questions.text: If L = {a, b}, then L* contains:
options: The empty string and all strings over {a, b}
Only the two strings a and b themselves
Every string except the empty string
Exactly two strings and nothing else
questions.shortExplanation: Kleene star includes ε and all combinations.
questions.explanation: The Kleene closure L* is the set of all strings formed by concatenating zero or more members of L, including the empty string.

questions.text: A string over an alphabet is:
options: A set of grammar production rules
An infinite sequence of symbols from the alphabet
questions.shortExplanation: A string is a finite symbol sequence.
questions.explanation: A string (or word) is a finite sequence of symbols taken from a given alphabet; its length is the number of symbols.

questions.text: The empty string is denoted by:
options: The symbol Σ used for the alphabet
questions.explanation: The empty string, written ε (epsilon), is the string of length zero containing no symbols.

questions.text: Which of the following is a prefix of the string 'compiler'?
questions.shortExplanation: A prefix is taken from the front.
questions.explanation: A prefix is obtained by removing zero or more symbols from the end, so 'comp' is a prefix of 'compiler' while 'piler' is a suffix.

questions.text: Finite automata are equal in expressive power to:
options: The context-free grammars used in parsing
questions.explanation: Finite automata and regular expressions describe exactly the same class of languages: the regular languages.

questions.text: A key limitation of a finite automaton is that it:
options: Has no memory beyond its current state
Contains no accepting states at all
Has no defined transitions between its states
Cannot have a designated start state
questions.explanation: A finite automaton cannot store unbounded information; its only memory is the current state, which is why it cannot match nested constructs.

questions.text: Converting a regular expression directly into an NFA is commonly done by:
options: Subset construction applied to the states
questions.shortExplanation: Thompson's construction builds an NFA from a regex.
questions.explanation: Thompson's construction builds an NFA (with ε-transitions) compositionally from the operators of a regular expression.

questions.text: Subset construction is the algorithm used to:
options: Remove left recursion from a grammar
Convert an NFA into an equivalent DFA
Minimize the number of DFA states
questions.explanation: Subset (powerset) construction creates DFA states from sets of NFA states, producing a DFA that accepts the same language.

questions.text: An ε-transition in an NFA lets the automaton:
options: Push a symbol onto an auxiliary stack
Read two input symbols in a single move
questions.explanation: An ε-transition moves the NFA from one state to another without reading any input symbol.

questions.text: A dead (trap) state in a DFA is a state that:
options: Is always chosen as the start state
Accepts the empty string by default
Has the largest number of outgoing transitions
Can never reach an accepting state
questions.shortExplanation: A dead state cannot reach acceptance.
questions.explanation: Once a DFA enters a dead state it can never reach an accepting state, so the remaining input is rejected.

questions.text: DFA minimization produces a DFA that:
options: Accepts a strictly larger language than before
Recognizes the same language with the fewest states
questions.shortExplanation: Minimization yields the smallest equivalent DFA.
questions.explanation: Minimization merges equivalent states to give the unique DFA with the minimum number of states for that language.

questions.text: Compared with an NFA, a DFA is usually preferred for implementation because it:
options: Runs faster with a single deterministic path
Recognizes a strictly larger class of languages
Always uses fewer states than the NFA
questions.explanation: A DFA has exactly one transition per symbol per state, so it can be simulated quickly without exploring multiple paths, even though it may have more states.

questions.text: A regular definition is useful because it allows you to:
options: Name regular expressions and reuse them
questions.shortExplanation: Regular definitions name and reuse regexes.
questions.explanation: A regular definition assigns names to regular expressions so that those names can be referenced when defining more complex token patterns.

questions.text: The 'maximal munch' (longest match) rule says the scanner should choose the:
options: First pattern listed, regardless of length
Shortest lexeme that matches some pattern
questions.explanation: When several prefixes match, the scanner selects the longest one (maximal munch), so '>=' is read as one token rather than '>' then '='.

questions.text: When two patterns match the same longest lexeme, the tie is broken by:
options: Choosing the pattern with the shortest name
Building a parse tree for both
Rejecting the input as a lexical error
The order in which the patterns are listed
questions.explanation: Scanner generators resolve ties by giving priority to the pattern listed first, which is how keywords are preferred over identifiers.

questions.text: Keywords such as 'while' and 'if' are usually:
options: Treated exactly like ordinary user identifiers
Discarded by the scanner before parsing
questions.explanation: Reserved keywords are recognized as their own tokens, taking priority over the identifier pattern they would otherwise match.

questions.text: Which of the following CANNOT be described by a regular expression?
questions.shortExplanation: Nesting needs more than regular power.
questions.explanation: Matching arbitrarily nested, balanced parentheses requires counting, which finite automata cannot do, so it is not a regular language.

questions.text: A transition diagram in lexical analysis is used to:
options: Model token recognition as states and edges
questions.explanation: A transition diagram depicts states and labeled edges that the scanner follows to recognize patterns and emit tokens.

questions.text: The class of regular languages is closed under:
questions.shortExplanation: Closed under union, concat, and star.
questions.explanation: The class of regular languages is closed under union, concatenation, and Kleene closure (and also complement and intersection).

questions.text: The alternation operator '|' in a regular expression expresses:
options: Concatenation of two symbols in order
questions.explanation: The '|' operator denotes alternation, matching either the expression on its left or the one on its right.

questions.text: The optional operator '?' applied to r means:
options: One or more occurrences of r in sequence
Zero or more occurrences of r
questions.explanation: The '?' operator makes the preceding expression optional, matching it either zero or one time.

questions.text: A lexical analyzer typically discards:
options: Identifiers and numeric constants in the program
questions.explanation: The scanner removes white space and comments because they carry no token meaning, passing only significant tokens to the parser.

questions.text: In panic-mode lexical recovery, the scanner:
options: Deletes characters until a valid token can start
Builds an NFA for the bad input
Rewrites the grammar of the language
questions.shortExplanation: Panic mode skips characters to recover.
questions.explanation: In panic-mode lexical recovery, the scanner deletes offending characters until it can begin matching a legal token again.

questions.text: A right-linear grammar generates exactly the:
questions.explanation: Right-linear (and left-linear) regular grammars generate exactly the regular languages, the same class as regular expressions and finite automata.

questions.text: A context-free grammar is formally defined by:
options: A set of states, an alphabet, and transitions
A collection of tokens and a symbol table
Terminals, nonterminals, a start symbol, and productions
questions.explanation: A CFG comprises a set of nonterminals, a set of terminals, a set of productions, and a designated start symbol.

questions.text: A sentential form is:
options: A finished sentence of terminals only
A string of terminals and/or nonterminals derivable from the start symbol
questions.explanation: A sentential form is any string derivable from the start symbol; if it contains only terminals, it is a sentence of the language.

questions.text: A rightmost derivation expands, at each step, the:
options: Leftmost nonterminal in the current form
questions.shortExplanation: Rightmost derivation expands the rightmost nonterminal.
questions.explanation: In a rightmost derivation, the rightmost nonterminal of the current sentential form is replaced at each step.

questions.text: Reading the leaves of a parse tree from left to right gives its:
questions.shortExplanation: Leaves give the yield of the tree.
questions.explanation: The yield (or frontier) of a parse tree is the sentence formed by concatenating its leaf symbols from left to right.

questions.text: The classic 'dangling else' problem is an example of:
questions.explanation: The dangling-else grammar allows an 'else' to attach to more than one 'if', producing multiple parse trees, which is ambiguity.

questions.text: Which production shows immediate left recursion?
questions.shortExplanation: A → Aα is immediate left recursion.
questions.explanation: A production whose right side begins with the same nonterminal on the left (A → Aα) is immediate left recursion, which breaks top-down parsing.

questions.text: Left factoring is applied when two productions for a nonterminal:
options: Begin from two different start symbols
questions.shortExplanation: Left factoring removes a common prefix.
questions.explanation: Left factoring rewrites productions that share a common leading prefix so a predictive parser can defer the choice until the prefix is consumed.

questions.text: A grammar is LL(1) when, for each nonterminal, its productions have:
options: Identical FIRST sets for all alternatives
No terminal symbols on the right side
questions.explanation: An LL(1) grammar lets a single lookahead token uniquely choose a production because the relevant FIRST (and FOLLOW for ε) sets are disjoint.

questions.text: A non-recursive predictive parser is driven by:
options: A finite automaton on its own with no stack
A pushdown stack but no table
A stack and a parsing table
questions.shortExplanation: Table-driven LL parser uses stack + table.
questions.explanation: A table-driven predictive parser uses an explicit stack and an LL(1) parsing table to decide which production to apply on each lookahead.

questions.text: Bottom-up parsing constructs the parse tree:
options: From the leaves up to the root
From the root downward to the leaves
Only at the root, left to right
questions.shortExplanation: Bottom-up builds from leaves to root.
questions.explanation: Bottom-up parsers begin with the input tokens (leaves) and reduce them step by step until reaching the start symbol (root).

questions.text: A bottom-up parser effectively traces a rightmost derivation:
options: Going forward in the usual direction
questions.explanation: Each reduction in shift-reduce parsing corresponds to one step of a rightmost derivation done in reverse.

questions.text: Repeatedly locating a handle and reducing it is called:
questions.explanation: Handle pruning is the sequence of locating handles and replacing them with the left side of the matching production until the start symbol remains.

questions.text: In LR parsing, a viable prefix is:
options: Any arbitrary string of terminal symbols
A prefix of a right-sentential form that can appear on the stack
questions.shortExplanation: Viable prefixes can sit on the stack.
questions.explanation: A viable prefix is a prefix of a right-sentential form that does not extend past the right end of the rightmost handle, so it is valid on the stack.

questions.text: Before constructing LR item sets, the grammar is first:
options: Left factored to remove common prefixes
Augmented with a new start production
questions.explanation: LR parser construction adds a new start symbol S' with S' → S so that acceptance can be detected by reducing this single augmenting production.

questions.text: An LR(0) item is a production together with a:
options: Dot marking the position parsed so far
Copy of the entire FOLLOW set
Lookahead terminal set attached to it
questions.shortExplanation: An item has a dot position.
questions.explanation: An LR(0) item is a production augmented with a dot indicating the position up to which the right-hand side has been recognized.

questions.text: Ordering these parsing methods from least to most powerful gives:
options: LALR, then SLR, then canonical LR(1)
Canonical LR(1), then LALR, then SLR
SLR, then canonical LR(1), then LALR
questions.explanation: SLR is the weakest, LALR is intermediate (and table-size efficient), and canonical LR(1) is the most powerful of the three.

questions.text: A shift-reduce conflict means the parser cannot decide whether to:
options: Accept the input or reject it outright
Read from or write to memory
questions.explanation: A shift-reduce conflict arises when, in some state, the parser could legally either shift the next input symbol or perform a reduction.

questions.text: By default, a YACC-style parser generator resolves a shift-reduce conflict by:
options: Selecting one of the actions at random
Reporting an error and halting the build
Performing the reduction instead of shifting
questions.explanation: Tools such as YACC resolve a shift-reduce conflict in favor of shift unless precedence and associativity declarations specify otherwise.

questions.text: An LR parsing table is divided into two parts called:
questions.shortExplanation: LR tables have ACTION and GOTO.
questions.explanation: The ACTION part decides shift/reduce/accept on terminals, while the GOTO part gives the next state for nonterminals.

questions.text: Context-free languages are recognized by a:
options: Plain finite automaton with no extra memory
questions.explanation: A pushdown automaton adds a stack to a finite automaton, giving it the memory needed to recognize context-free languages such as nested structures.

questions.text: In the Chomsky hierarchy, context-free grammars are:
questions.explanation: In the Chomsky hierarchy, Type 2 grammars are context-free; Type 3 are regular, Type 1 context-sensitive, and Type 0 unrestricted.

questions.text: Which of the following is a unit production?
questions.shortExplanation: A → B is a unit production.
questions.explanation: A unit production has a single nonterminal on its right-hand side and can often be eliminated to simplify a grammar.

questions.text: An ε-production is a production whose right-hand side is:
questions.explanation: An ε-production (A → ε) lets a nonterminal derive the empty string and affects the computation of FIRST and FOLLOW sets.

questions.text: A grammar symbol that can never derive any terminal string is called:
options: A handle on the parser stack
questions.explanation: A non-generating symbol cannot derive a terminal string and is one kind of useless symbol that can be removed from a grammar.

questions.text: Recursive-descent parsing without lookahead may require:
options: Storing the stack on secondary disk
Minimization of a deterministic finite automaton
questions.explanation: A general recursive-descent parser may try a production, fail, and back up to try another, which predictive parsing avoids.

questions.text: Operator-precedence parsing is a form of:
questions.explanation: Operator-precedence parsing is a shift-reduce (bottom-up) technique that uses precedence relations between terminals to find handles.

questions.text: In panic-mode recovery, a parser discards tokens until it reaches a:
options: Randomly chosen token in the stream
Copy of the grammar's start symbol
questions.shortExplanation: It skips to a synchronizing token.
questions.explanation: Panic-mode error recovery skips tokens until one from a chosen synchronizing set appears, letting the parser resume in a stable position.

questions.text: Left recursion in a grammar is directly unsuitable for which method?
options: Bottom-up LR parsing of the input
questions.explanation: Left recursion causes a top-down predictive parser to loop forever, so it must be eliminated; LR parsers handle left recursion fine.

questions.text: The goal of parsing is to:
options: Strip white space from the input
Check that the tokens conform to the grammar
Translate the program into machine code
questions.shortExplanation: Parsing checks syntax and builds structure.
questions.explanation: The parser checks whether the sequence of tokens forms a valid sentence of the language and produces a parse or syntax tree.

questions.text: Two distinct rightmost derivations of the same sentence indicate that the grammar is:
questions.explanation: A grammar is ambiguous if some sentence has more than one parse tree (equivalently, more than one leftmost or rightmost derivation).

questions.text: FIRST(α) is the set of:
options: Nonterminals reachable from the string α
Terminals that can begin a string derived from α
All productions defined for the start symbol
questions.explanation: FIRST(α) contains every terminal that can appear as the first symbol of some string derived from α, plus ε if α can derive the empty string.

questions.text: FOLLOW(A) is the set of terminals that can appear:
options: Only within accepting states of a DFA
Immediately to the right of A in some sentential form
Anywhere inside the compiler's symbol table
Only at the very start of the whole program
questions.explanation: FOLLOW(A) is the set of terminals that can immediately follow the nonterminal A in some sentential form derived from the start symbol.

questions.text: The end-of-input marker '$' is normally placed in the FOLLOW set of the:
options: First terminal token of the program
questions.shortExplanation: $ is in FOLLOW of the start symbol.
questions.explanation: Because input ends after the start symbol's derivation, the end-of-input marker $ is placed in FOLLOW of the start symbol.

questions.text: In LL(1) table construction, A → α is entered under each terminal in:
options: FIRST(α), plus FOLLOW(A) if α derives ε
The set of all DFA states
questions.shortExplanation: Use FIRST(α), plus FOLLOW(A) for ε.
questions.explanation: A → α is placed under each terminal in FIRST(α); if α derives ε, it is also placed under each terminal in FOLLOW(A).

questions.text: A reduce-reduce conflict means a state allows reduction by:
options: Exactly one production and no other
questions.explanation: A reduce-reduce conflict occurs when the parser, in one state on one lookahead, could reduce by more than one production.

questions.text: A parser that scans left to right and produces a leftmost derivation is an:
questions.explanation: The first L in LL means left-to-right scanning and the second L means it produces a leftmost derivation, characteristic of top-down predictive parsers.

questions.text: LALR parsing is popular in practice mainly because it:
options: Combines small tables with adequate power
Needs no grammar specification at all
Is the single most powerful parsing method known
questions.shortExplanation: LALR balances power and table size.
questions.explanation: LALR merges canonical LR(1) states with common cores, giving much smaller tables than full LR(1) while handling most practical grammars.

questions.text: The CLOSURE operation on a set of LR items adds items for:
options: Every terminal symbol of the grammar
Productions of nonterminals just after the dot
All FOLLOW sets in the grammar
questions.explanation: CLOSURE adds, for every nonterminal immediately to the right of a dot, the initial items of that nonterminal's productions.

questions.text: A predictive parser detects a syntax error when:
options: The parsing stack becomes completely full
The start symbol is first pushed on the stack
The table entry for the current pair is empty
Any input token at all is read
questions.shortExplanation: Empty table entry signals an error.
questions.explanation: If the LL(1) table has no production for the top-of-stack nonterminal and current lookahead, no legal move exists, signalling a syntax error.

questions.text: Eliminating left recursion from A → A α | β produces:
options: A → β A', A' → α A' | ε
A → ε as the only production
questions.shortExplanation: Introduce A' for the recursive tail.
questions.explanation: The standard transformation rewrites left recursion into right recursion using a new nonterminal: A → β A' with A' → α A' | ε.

questions.text: A syntax-directed definition (SDD) attaches to grammar productions:
options: Machine instructions for the target processor
Token patterns written as regular expressions
questions.shortExplanation: SDDs attach semantic rules to productions.
questions.explanation: An SDD associates each production with semantic rules that define how attribute values of grammar symbols are computed.

questions.text: A synthesized attribute of a node is computed from the attributes of its:
options: Parent node and its sibling nodes
Entry stored in the symbol table
questions.explanation: Synthesized attributes flow up the tree: a node's synthesized attribute is computed from the attributes of its child nodes.

questions.text: An inherited attribute of a node gets its value from its:
questions.explanation: Inherited attributes flow down or across the tree, taking their values from the parent node and/or sibling nodes.

questions.text: A definition that uses only synthesized attributes is called:
questions.explanation: An S-attributed definition uses solely synthesized attributes and can be evaluated during a bottom-up parse.

questions.text: S-attributed definitions are naturally evaluated during a:
options: Pass of lexical analysis over characters
questions.explanation: Because synthesized attributes depend only on children, they can be computed on reductions during bottom-up parsing.

questions.text: In an L-attributed definition, an inherited attribute may depend on:
options: Right siblings and the node's own subtree
questions.explanation: In an L-attributed SDD, each inherited attribute depends only on the parent and the siblings to its left, allowing a single left-to-right pass.

questions.text: An annotated parse tree is one in which each node also shows its:
questions.explanation: An annotated (decorated) parse tree displays the computed attribute values at the nodes alongside the grammar symbols.

questions.text: A dependency graph for an SDD is used to find:
options: A valid evaluation order for the attributes
The total number of tokens in the program
The number of machine registers needed
A minimized form of the DFA
questions.explanation: The dependency graph records how attributes depend on one another; a topological sort of it gives an order in which they can be evaluated.

questions.text: An abstract syntax tree (AST) differs from a parse tree because it:
options: Keeps a node for every single grammar symbol used
Is constructed entirely by the loader
questions.explanation: An abstract syntax tree condenses a parse tree by removing nodes that exist only for grammar derivation, keeping the meaningful operators and operands.

questions.text: Type checking, part of semantic analysis, verifies that:
options: The input buffers are sized correctly
The number of tokens is within a limit
Every keyword in the program is spelled correctly
questions.explanation: A type checker confirms that each operator receives operands of permitted types and reports type errors otherwise.

questions.text: Automatically converting an int to a float when needed is an example of:
questions.explanation: Type coercion is the implicit conversion the compiler inserts so operands of mixed types can be combined, such as widening an int to a float.

questions.text: Under name equivalence, two types are the same only if they:
options: Are combined by the same operator
Possess exactly the same internal structure
Occupy the same region of memory
questions.explanation: Name equivalence treats two types as equal only when they share the same type name, unlike structural equivalence which compares their structure.

questions.text: The two fundamental operations on a symbol table are:
options: Shift and reduce performed by the parser
Open and close on a file
Push and pop on a parsing stack
questions.shortExplanation: Symbol tables insert and look up entries.
questions.explanation: A symbol table chiefly supports inserting new identifier entries and looking up existing ones during the various phases.

questions.text: Using an identifier that was never declared is detected as a:
options: Lexical error in the character stream
questions.shortExplanation: Undeclared use is a semantic error.
questions.explanation: Detecting use of an undeclared identifier requires symbol-table information, so it is a semantic (static-semantic) error.

questions.text: In a block-structured language, the scope of a variable is the:
options: Whole program from beginning to end, always
Region where its declaration is visible
Contents of the compiler's symbol table
Complete set of tokens in the file
questions.shortExplanation: Scope is where a name is visible.
questions.explanation: Scope is the textual region in which a declaration applies; nested blocks create nested scopes that the symbol table must track.

questions.text: Static scoping determines a name's meaning based on the:
options: Sequence of calls made at run time
Order in which the scanner reads tokens
questions.explanation: Under static (lexical) scoping, a name refers to the declaration found by examining the enclosing program text, independent of run-time call chains.

questions.text: Calling a function with the wrong number of arguments is a:
options: Lexical error in the token stream
Purely syntactic error caught by the grammar
Defect that can never be detected by a compiler
questions.explanation: Comparing a call against the declared parameter list is a semantic check, so an argument-count mismatch is a semantic error.

questions.text: A directed acyclic graph (DAG) is used for an expression to:
options: Remove the start symbol of the grammar
Add strictly more nodes than the corresponding tree
questions.explanation: A DAG representation of an expression lets identical subexpressions share a single node, exposing redundancy for later use.

questions.text: A type expression such as array(integer) is used to:
options: Describe the type of a construct
questions.explanation: A type expression is a notation (built from basic types and constructors like array, record, and pointer) that denotes the type of a construct.

questions.text: Postfix (reverse Polish) notation for an expression is produced by a:
options: Preorder traversal of the expression tree
questions.explanation: Visiting an expression tree in postorder (operands before operator) yields the postfix form of the expression.

questions.text: In YACC, the semantic value of a rule's left-hand side is written as:
questions.explanation: In YACC actions, $$ denotes the attribute of the rule's left-hand nonterminal, while $1, $2, ... refer to the right-hand symbols.

questions.text: Replacing 3 + 4 with the constant 7 at compile time is called:
questions.explanation: Constant folding evaluates constant expressions during compilation so the result is stored directly instead of being computed at run time.

questions.text: Quadruples and triples are alternative representations of:
options: Regular expressions used by the scanner
Parse trees built by the parser
questions.explanation: Quadruples and triples are common ways to store three-address instructions, differing in how they reference temporary results.

questions.text: Semantic actions in a translation scheme are written:
options: Inside the loader of the system
Only before the grammar, never inside it
questions.explanation: A translation scheme embeds program fragments (semantic actions) at positions within the right-hand sides of productions to indicate execution order.

questions.text: An attribute recording the data type of an expression is typically:
options: A state of the recognizing DFA
A token pattern in the scanner
An inherited attribute passed down from the parent
questions.explanation: The type of an expression is generally synthesized bottom-up from the types of its operands, making it a synthesized attribute.

questions.text: Nested scopes are commonly handled by organizing the symbol table as a:
options: Single flat list of all identifiers
questions.shortExplanation: Nested scopes use a stack of tables.
questions.explanation: Block structure is commonly implemented with a stack of symbol tables (or chained scopes) so that entering and leaving a block pushes and pops a scope.

questions.text: An attribute grammar is a context-free grammar augmented with:
questions.explanation: An attribute grammar extends a context-free grammar by associating attributes with symbols and semantic rules with productions.

questions.text: Declaring the same variable twice in one scope is reported as a:
questions.explanation: The symbol table reveals that an identifier is already declared in the current scope, so a re-declaration is flagged as a semantic error.

questions.text: Under structural type equivalence, two types are equal when they:
options: Happen to share the same type name
Are built using the same operator
Are declared inside the same block
questions.explanation: Structural equivalence considers two types the same if their type expressions have identical structure, even when their names differ.

questions.text: The information stored for an identifier in the symbol table typically includes its:
options: Final object-code address and nothing else
questions.shortExplanation: Symbol table holds type, scope, etc.
questions.explanation: A symbol-table entry records attributes such as the identifier's type, scope/level, storage information, and possibly its value.

questions.text: A bottom-up parser keeps its partially recognized symbols on a:
questions.explanation: Shift-reduce parsing pushes symbols onto a stack and reduces handles found on top of that stack.

questions.text: Which pair of phases is most tightly coupled in a syntax-directed translator?
options: Linking of modules and loading into memory
questions.explanation: A syntax-directed translator interleaves semantic actions with parsing, so parsing and semantic analysis run hand in hand.

questions.text: A scanner generator such as LEX takes regular expressions and produces a:
questions.shortExplanation: LEX builds a scanner from regexes.
questions.explanation: LEX-style tools transform regular-expression specifications into a finite-automaton-based lexical analyzer.

questions.text: A parser generator such as YACC takes a grammar and produces a:
questions.shortExplanation: YACC builds a parser from a grammar.
questions.explanation: YACC-style tools take a context-free grammar with actions and generate a bottom-up (LALR) parser.

questions.text: An LR parser reaches the accept action when it:
options: Empties the input buffer of all characters
Reduces by the augmenting start production
Shifts the very first token onto the stack
Enters a dead state of the automaton
questions.explanation: An LR parser accepts when it performs the accept action, which corresponds to reducing by the added S' → S production with the end marker.

questions.text: Which statement about a leftmost derivation is true?
options: It can never generate an ambiguous string
It produces only terminals at every single step
It expands the rightmost nonterminal at each step
It always rewrites the leftmost nonterminal first
questions.explanation: In a leftmost derivation, the leftmost nonterminal of the current sentential form is the one rewritten at each step.

questions.text: Lexical and syntax analysis are kept separate mainly to:
options: Simplify the design of each component
Eliminate the need for any grammar
Maximize the total number of tokens produced
Avoid building a symbol table altogether
questions.explanation: Splitting scanning from parsing simplifies each component, lets specialized techniques (regular vs context-free) apply, and improves efficiency and portability.

questions.text: A handle in a right-sentential form is:
options: Any leftmost terminal of the form
The grammar's start symbol by itself
A substring matching a production's right side, reduced next
questions.shortExplanation: A handle is the next substring to reduce.
questions.explanation: A handle is a substring that matches the right side of a production and whose reduction represents one step of the reverse rightmost derivation.

questions.text: Which statement about NFAs and DFAs is correct?
options: DFAs recognize strictly more languages than NFAs can
An NFA can never be converted into a DFA
They recognize exactly the same class of languages
A DFA may have several transitions on one symbol
questions.shortExplanation: NFAs and DFAs are equally powerful.
questions.explanation: Although NFAs may be more compact, they recognize exactly the regular languages, the same class DFAs recognize, and every NFA has an equivalent DFA.

questions.text: A production such as A → A (the same nonterminal alone) introduces a:
questions.explanation: A production such as A → A introduces a cycle in the grammar, which must be removed because it serves no purpose and complicates parsing.

questions.text: A typical use of an inherited attribute is to pass down:
options: A declared type to the identifiers it declares
The computed value of a child expression
A token's source line number only
The number of states in the scanning DFA
questions.shortExplanation: Inherited attributes pass declaration types down.
questions.explanation: A typical use of inherited attributes is to carry a declared type from a declaration node down to each identifier being declared.

questions.text: Which compiler phase is specified using context-free grammars?
options: Loading of the program into memory
Lexical analysis of the character stream
questions.explanation: Syntax analysis is specified by context-free grammars, whereas lexical analysis is specified by regular expressions.

questions.text: Which of the following is checked by static (compile-time) semantics?
options: The contents of memory while running
How long the program runs when executed
Whether a variable is declared before use
The exact runtime value held by a variable
questions.explanation: Static semantics covers properties checkable at compile time, such as declaration before use and type correctness, not run-time values.

questions.text: When a top-down parser predicts the wrong production and must undo work, it performs:
options: A closure of the item set
A shift of the next symbol
questions.shortExplanation: Undoing a wrong prediction is backtracking.
questions.explanation: Backtracking is the act of reversing a tried production choice in a top-down parser so an alternative can be attempted.

questions.text: Which sequence correctly lists data flowing through the front-end?
options: Characters → tokens → parse tree → annotated tree
questions.shortExplanation: Chars → tokens → parse tree → annotated tree.
questions.explanation: The scanner turns characters into tokens, the parser builds a parse tree, and semantic analysis decorates it, so the data flows in that order.

questions.text: An augmented grammar is needed in LR parsing so the parser can:
options: Operate completely without using a stack
Recognize when the whole input is parsed
Remove every terminal from the grammar
questions.shortExplanation: Augmentation enables a clean accept action.
questions.explanation: Adding S' → S gives the parser a unique production whose reduction signals that the entire input has been parsed, defining acceptance.

questions.text: A lexical analyzer commonly interacts with the parser by:
options: Returning the next token on request
Returning the complete token list only at the very end
Building the entire parse tree by itself
questions.explanation: Commonly the scanner acts as a subroutine of the parser, supplying the next token whenever the parser asks for one.

questions.text: Which task is performed during semantic analysis rather than parsing?
options: Building the parse tree from tokens
Verifying that an array index is an integer
Checking that brackets are grammatically balanced
questions.shortExplanation: Type of an index is a semantic check.
questions.explanation: Confirming that an array index is an integer requires type information and is a semantic check, while bracket balance is syntactic.

questions.text: Two grammars that generate exactly the same language are said to be:
questions.explanation: Grammars are equivalent when they generate the same language, even if their productions or derivations differ.

questions.text: The overall purpose of the compiler front-end is to:
options: Produce optimized target machine code for the processor
Load the program and run it on the machine
Resolve external references to library functions
Analyze the source and produce a checked IR
questions.shortExplanation: Front-end analyzes and yields a checked IR.
questions.explanation: The front-end scans, parses, and semantically checks the source program, producing an intermediate representation for the back-end to translate.
